title: "Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it"
---

[Lecture slides](../lectures/15-descriptive-report/lec.qmd) · [Weekly self-check](quiz.qmd)


## Today's question

Can a reader understand the seedling measurements, their variation, and the limits
of our description? A useful biological report does not need a significance test
on every page. Today you will make the data handling, figure, summary, and
interpretation fit together.

Save a new source document, `descriptive-report.Rmd`, at the project root. You
may copy your first report's structure, but deliberately revise its methods and
interpretation. Keep `data/` paths relative to this root. The supplied measurements
are simulated. Plants received a control or nutrient treatment and were measured
seven days apart; the nutrient formulation is unspecified.

Produce **one** descriptive report today. The teacher may choose the organic
laboratory alternative below instead of the seedling report. In that case save
`organic-report.Rmd` at the same project root and use its stated variables and
units throughout; do not mix the two datasets in one set of results.

## Choose and state which input you use

Use **`data/seedlings.csv` for the core report**. It contains 24 complete plant
records. Include a data-quality note explaining the checks you performed: unique
plant IDs, allowed treatment labels, numeric length columns, and missing-value
counts. A statement that “R loaded the file” is not a data-quality check.

If the teacher asks you to report the repaired day 11 data instead, include the
repair code or source it from a saved script within the project. Do not read a
derived file that cannot be recreated from the shared raw data. State which
source you used and retain the unavailable P06 observation; do not silently mix
results from the repaired and complete datasets.

## Build the report in a clear order

Use this order inside the report:

1. Load packages and import the input file.
2. Inspect its structure and document relevant data checks.
3. Derive `growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm`.
4. Calculate the grouped summary with sample counts, mean, median, and SD.
5. Draw the individual-plant figure with group means.
6. Explain the centre, spread, overlap, and limitations in ordinary language.

Here is a compact data-check block that can appear after import:

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anyDuplicated(seedlings$plant_id)
seedlings |> count(treatment)
sum(is.na(seedlings$initial_mm))
sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
```

`anyDuplicated()` returns zero when it finds no duplicate; a positive result
identifies the position of the first duplicate, not a count of duplicates.
Include only checking output that helps the reader, but keep the code available
in the source. Reuse your day 13 summary and figure rather than replacing them
with a screenshot of the RStudio Environment pane.

A table in an R Markdown chunk can be displayed neatly with:

```{r}
group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(group_summary, digits = 2,
             caption = "Observed growth and variation by treatment; lengths in mm.")
```

The table is generated from code. If the data change, the rendered table can
change too. A caption must distinguish SD among plants from uncertainty in the
mean. This report has SD, not confidence intervals.

## Write with the question in view

A useful description distinguishes three ideas: group averages differ in this
sample; plants vary within each group; and sample descriptions do not quantify
all uncertainty about a treatment effect. You can report observed values with
units and identify the independent unit without declaring a universal result.

For the complete data, the group means are about 15.3 mm for controls and 21.5 mm
for treated plants. Check your table rather than copying these numbers into
prose without verification. The treated group also has more spread in these
data. Do not say that every treated plant outgrew every control plant: the
individual observations overlap.

## Alternative context: report collected-product yield

Use this in place of the seedling report if selected. The question is: **what
percentage of the supplied maximum product mass was collected in each run, and
how does it vary between protocols?** All data are simulated. A synthesis run
is one independently carried-out product-making experiment. Twelve independent
runs were randomly assigned to two protocols, six to each. A protocol is a
specified method; no knowledge of its chemical steps is required here.

`theoretical_mass_g` is the supplied maximum possible product mass for that
run's starting amounts. `isolated_mass_g` is the dry collected product mass,
assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Both are in grams. Calculate
percentage yield with `100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g`, so Y01 is
`100 * 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%`. Theoretical masses differ with starting scale;
compare the percentages, not the raw masses. You do not need to balance a
reaction or calculate a theoretical mass yourself.

```{r}
organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
organic_summary <- organic |>
  group_by(protocol) |>
  summarise(n_runs = n(), mean_yield_percent = mean(yield_percent),
            sd_percentage_points = sd(yield_percent), .groups = "drop")
organic_summary
```

Follow the same report order: import and check IDs, labels, numeric masses,
missing values, and positive theoretical masses; calculate yield; show a table
and individual-run plot; then interpret centre, spread, and overlap. Both groups
have six available runs. Mean yields are about 68.67% and 77.00%; SDs are about
4.32 and 3.74 **percentage points** for standard and modified protocols.
Label the y-axis “Isolated product yield (%)” and identify one point as one run.
Do not call repeated weighings of one product batch independent runs.

This is descriptive work: no t-test is needed. A higher mean yield does not
establish greater purity, safety, environmental benefit, or superiority in other
reactions. Write a limitation tied to the small simulated set and the assumed
purity. Keep the source and data together so the report can render from scratch.

## Your practical and a reader check

1. Complete the report with a question, data/design paragraph, methods, table,
   figure, and interpretation. Keep it short enough that each part earns its place.
2. Include the number of independent plants, or independent synthesis runs for
   the alternative, and state what the figure's symbols represent. Name any
   exclusions or missing measurements.
3. Restart R and run this command in the **R Console**, not in a code chunk
   inside the report (a report must not try to render itself):

```{r}
rmarkdown::render("descriptive-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")
```

For the organic alternative, replace the quoted filename with
`"organic-report.Rmd"`; render only the report you chose.

4. Ask a partner to read the HTML. Can they identify the units, input file,
   observational unit, main pattern, and main limitation without opening RStudio?
5. If remote R access is available, locate the project on that computer and
   repeat the render there using the supplied connection instructions. First
   identify whether the R session and data are local or remote. Otherwise,
   repeat from a newly opened local project; do not invent connection details.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: reproducibility is a file relationship

An HTML file beside an `.Rmd` is not enough if the source expects data in your
personal Downloads folder. Keep the documented project structure, original data,
and source together. The fresh-session render reveals missing dependencies.
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A good limitation is specific

“The sample is small” is less informative than naming the independent unit,
noting overlap or variation, and explaining that today's report describes the
sample without yet estimating uncertainty in a treatment difference. Missing
observations, when present, should also be counted and discussed.
:::

## Extended practical — edit a report as a reader, then as an analyst

Plan 75–90 minutes of revision of the one descriptive report you selected.
Do not create a second compulsory biology/chemistry report just to make the
session longer. The goal is a complete short scientific account with a traceable
analysis, not more headings or a longer printout. Save a revision log in
`reports/day15-revision.txt` alongside your own report source at project root.

1. Read only the rendered HTML, with the code initially closed. Write down the
   question, independent unit, input filename, measurement or derived outcome,
   and units. If any cannot be found, add a specific sentence or label rather
   than relying on the reader to infer it from an object name.
2. Inspect every numerical statement. Match it to the code and table that
   produced it. Check n against available observations, not all lines in a
   CSV. Record whether you used complete seedling data, the repaired exercise,
   or the independent organic-run context, and carry that choice through all
   counts, captions, and limitations.
3. Replace three weak sentences. Use these starting examples: “The results
   were good”; “the treatment had more error”; “the computer removed the bad
   values.” Your replacements must identify a measured pattern, a defined
   quantity such as SD, or an evidence-supported action. Avoid claiming an
   effect has been tested in this descriptive report.
4. Check that the figure shows observations with units. Identify what each
   summary symbol means. Put the figure beside a small table that answers a
   complementary question; remove redundant raw printouts if they do not help
   a reader. More pages are not automatically more reproducible.
5. Add two inline values in the results prose using the R Markdown pattern
   already introduced: one count and one mean or SD. Test them by rendering.
   The object must be created earlier inside the document. Keep interpretation
   in ordinary prose rather than assuming inline code writes a conclusion.
6. Ask a partner to reproduce the report from a complete project copy. If
   working alone, extract a fresh course folder in a new temporary location,
   add your source and required inputs, and render there. Record the first
   failure before fixing it. A relative input path is useful only if the
   needed data file was actually included.
7. Save the revised HTML and its `.Rmd` source. Write a compact change log:
   issue, evidence, correction, and rerun result. Keep the previous source as
   a clearly named backup or ordinary copied file, without inventing a
   complicated version-control workflow.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: separate numerical checks from wording checks

The complete seedling table has 24 plants; the repaired exercise has 24 plant
records but 23 observed growths. The organic alternative has 12 independent
runs, six per protocol, with no missing masses. A report may use any selected
route, but cannot switch silently between these denominators. Use the Console
for a `rmarkdown::render()` call; never put a self-render command into the report.
:::

## Independent transfer — a new class asks for a concise descriptive report

Allow 60–90 minutes, extending to another session if rendering needs support.
The new class supplies `data/seedlings-transfer.csv`: 18 independent potted
plants, nine randomly assigned to each allocation, initial and final lengths
in mm seven days apart. The task is to **describe** growth and its variation;
it is not yet a request for a significance test.

1. Create `transfer-description.Rmd` in the project root. Start from your
   chosen source's structure, but remove old imports, variable names, numbers,
   and biological descriptions that no longer apply. A template is a structure
   to adapt, not evidence that the old findings describe new observations.
2. State the new question, independent unit, input, units, and growth formula.
   Include checks for identifiers, group counts, and missingness in the saved
   source. If you used the transfer dataset in earlier scripts, recreate its
   objects inside this report rather than depending on the Environment pane.
3. Produce one labelled individual-point figure and a group table with n,
   mean, median, and SD. Choose sensible rounding in the displayed table.
   Explain the distinction between the 18 input rows and the two summary rows.
4. Write 150–250 words of results and interpretation, using calculated numbers
   and one limitation. Address direction, overlap, and spread. Do not translate
   a higher mean into “every treated plant did better”, or SD into uncertainty
   in a difference. Independent comparison methods arrive in the next block.
5. Render after restarting and locate the actual output HTML. If you render
   into `reports/`, document that destination. Confirm that changing only the
   report title does not change its calculations, and that changing an input
   filename requires appropriate new checks and prose.
6. Make a one-page handover note listing the minimum files needed to reproduce
   the new report. Open the report on another computer if supported; otherwise
   use a separately located project copy. Record which kind of portability
   check you actually performed, without claiming an untested environment.

**Additional outputs:** revised chosen report, revision log, the self-contained
transfer report and HTML, and the handover note. You should now be able to
explain both what the observations show and how a reader can regenerate them.

**Keep:** your chosen `descriptive-report.Rmd` or `organic-report.Rmd` and its
HTML, with the code and data needed to render it.
